items.t: Explainers. Every number has a source.
items.s: Short narrated films on the ideas behind the work, with every number sourced on screen and recall questions with spaced review.
Tallow, Pylon and Rerun host the explainer films: who they are, what each one stands for, and their introductions.
Night School teaches how AI works, from gradients to GPU kernels, in animated films and labs that run real models in your browser.
Night School's lessons drawn as lights along one coast at night. Every light links to its lesson; faint paths join the lessons that help first.
Watch Pylon turn crates into arrows, dot products and cosines, then drag them yourself and explore the attention model's own word table.
Watch Pylon's crane move the whole chart with a matrix, then drive it yourself and rebuild the attention model's question from its trained weights.
Pylon feels her way down a hill in fog: the gradient, a step that goes over the edge, a real model's loss, then you walk the hills yourself.
A chain of buckets down the hill: how a network gets every number's slope in one walk back, checked number by number, then trained in your browser.
Careful steps, a heavy ball and Adam race down the same valleys, then train a real network: who wins depends on the hill.
A curve that passes through every point and fails on new ones: overfitting, the held-out set, a leash, and how even a held-out score is one draw.
How a language model cuts text into pieces: letters, merges learned from counts (byte-pair encoding), and bytes so nothing is left on the dock.
How a list of numbers per word comes to mean something: the skip-gram learns places from the company words keep, measured against a shuffled control.

items.t: Night School: Next-word prediction and the loss
items.s: How a language model guesses the next word as a spread of belief, how softmax makes it, and how the loss scores it as surprise.
Watch Tallow show how attention lets a word use the words before it, then train a tiny transformer in your browser and watch its heads learn.
What one transformer block does: layer norm, attention, the MLP and the residual stream, taken apart room by room on a real model.
Batch, forward, loss, backward, step: the whole loop that trains a language model, rerun exactly, with one setting changed at a time.
The same model trained on different crates: how much of a skill's data it needs, what wrong labels and repeated rows do, and what it never saw.
Twelve small models of different sizes trained on the same text: what size buys, what more work buys, and what the scaling-law papers found.
How a language model's spread of belief becomes text: greedy choice, sampling, temperature, top-k and top-p, measured against the rules.

items.t: Night School: Evaluating a language model
items.s: One small model scored by loss, exact match and two judges, with error bars: where the scores agree, where they part, and how a leaked test fools them.
Train a small model on a big one's guesses instead of the text alone: when the teacher's soft answers help, and when the text is enough.
Store a model's weights in 8, 6, 4, 3 or 2 bits and measure what it loses: scales per table, per output and per group, and GPTQ's careful rounding.
Teach a trained model a new habit by changing every number, a few, or a pair of thin LoRA strips: what each learns, and what each forgets.

items.t: Night School: Our MMBU Challenge entry
items.s: Two weeks of fine-tuning a small model for a biomedical image contest: every bar written first, the misses kept, and what the logbook cannot prove.

Run a model with 16-bit numbers: where fp16 and bf16 can put a value, why sums stall, and what keeping the sums in 32 bits buys on held-out rows.
